extraction.research_question: Do legislators' social ties with political allies and political adversaries affect how they vote? Specifically, does more social connectedness predict more voting agreement between allies, and less agreement between adversaries (the "keep your friends close and enemies closer" logic)? (pp. 601-603, 609-610)
extraction.theory: Legislators use social contacts as information sources. Ties to allies are valuable when the two agree, and ties to adversaries are valuable when they disagree, because a predictable source of cues helps a legislator confirm or revise a policy position. Legislators therefore form expectations about whether a colleague will agree, and the link between connectedness and voting depends on those expectations (ideology and party are the basis for the expectations). Hypothesis 1: the more socially connected two political adversaries are, the less likely they are to vote the same way. Hypothesis 2: the more socially connected two political allies are, the more likely they are to vote the same way. The authors state the causal direction is simultaneous and endogenous (social ties can drive co-voting, and anticipated co-voting can drive ties) and limit claims to symmetric association (pp. 605-610, 620).
extraction.data: Population of interest: legislative staffers (assistants) of MEPs on the European Parliament's Committee on Environment, Public Health and Food Safety, 2004-2009 term. Network data: web questionnaire (8 responses) and interviews (24, June-July 2007) with staff of 32 of 65 committee members' offices (47% response; 3 members from Bulgaria and Romania were excluded because they joined in January 2007). Full dyadic census of the committee: 65 offices, 4,160 directed or 2,080 symmetric dyads. Dyadic response was 46% for directed reports (1,920 of 4,160) and 71.4% when reports on non-respondents' offices are used. Density was 5.7% on the respondent-alter subnetwork (9.7% if symmetrized) and 6.1% (118 of 1,920 possible ties) on the full asymmetric subnetwork. Voting data: 40 final plenary roll-call votes on Environment Committee bills plus amendments, July 2004 to July 2008 (sixth term). Analysed unit: dyad (pair of MEPs). Observations: 1,920 dyads with network information (1,912 in the OLS and linear models; 1,319 in the log-odds model after dropping 0% and 100% co-voting). Ideology: NOMINATE scores from Hix and Noury (sixth EP). Sample description and missingness tests: Tables 1-2.
extraction.method: Dependent variable is the co-voting rate per dyad (share of roll calls where both voted yes or both no). Model 1: OLS on all observations, presented as misspecified for comparison. Model 2: linear mixed-effects model (lmer, REML) with crossed random effects for respondent and alter, using all observations. Model 3: logit-transformed co-voting rate (log-odds) with random effects for respondent and alter, fitted with lmer and a Laplace approximation, dropping unanimous (0% and 100%) dyads. Predictors: same party, same voting bloc (GUE/NGL plus Greens/EFA vs PES, ALDE, UEN and EPP-ED, inferred from voting; four members belong to neither bloc), same nationality, absolute difference in seniority, point connectivity, and point connectivity x same bloc. Robustness: the authors estimated alternative specifications (lagged votes, joint-membership instrument, reverse-causality models) and report that results are sensitive to specification changes (fn. 81, p. 627); the chosen specification is defended as most theoretically consistent.
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. The authors acknowledge a simultaneity or reverse-causality problem (pp. 610, 620, 627). They address (a) non-independence of dyads with crossed random effects for respondent and alter (pp. 623-624), (b) reverse causation partly by controlling for expected co-voting through voting-bloc membership (p. 620), and (c) the ordinal/bounded outcome with a log-odds transform (p. 623). They assume non-respondents are missing at random, and they do not test this beyond comparing response by region (Table 1, chi-square 0.935, p = 0.817) and EU accession date (Table 2, chi-square 0.3752, p = 0.540) (pp. 614-616).
extraction.scope: Population: MEPs on one committee (Environment, Public Health and Food Safety) in the European Parliament, 2004-2009, and their staff networks. Policy area: environment and consumer protection (p. 613). Era: sixth parliamentary term (2004-2008 votes; 2007 survey). The authors frame the theory generally for legislatures (US and EP examples), but the data cover one committee in one policy area with 65 offices, so they caution about generalization (pp. 613, 627-628).

key_findings.finding: Hypothesis 1 supported: higher point connectivity between opposing-bloc MEPs predicts less frequent co-voting, and the coefficient is negative and distinguishable from zero in all three specifications, controlling for party and bloc.
key_findings.numbers: Point connectivity coefficient: OLS -0.0716 (SE 0.0043); linear multilevel -0.0234 (SE 0.0051); log-odds multilevel -0.1020 (SE 0.0307).

key_findings.finding: Log-odds effect size: a one-unit increase in point connectivity lowers the odds of co-voting by about 10 per cent for non-coalition pairs.
key_findings.numbers: Drop of 10% in odds (95% CI 7-13%). On the probability scale, moving from -1 SD (0.6) to +1 SD (3.8) connectivity lowers predicted co-voting for non-coalition pairs from 52% to 44%. A one-unit increase around the median (2) lowers it from 50% to 47%.

key_findings.finding: Baseline: with no social information, opposing-bloc members are predicted to vote together about half the time, which is the empirical mean for such dyads.
key_findings.numbers: Predicted co-voting about 50% at the empirical mean.

key_findings.finding: Same-bloc membership strongly predicts co-voting; joint party membership, nationality and seniority difference do not add explanatory power once bloc is controlled.
key_findings.numbers: Joint bloc membership: OLS 0.3552 (SE 0.0147); linear 0.5590 (SE 0.0135); log-odds 2.9103 (SE 0.0985), i.e., odds roughly 300% higher. Party: 0.0164 / 0.0063 / -0.0953 (none significant). Nationality and seniority: not significant.

key_findings.finding: Hypothesis 2 (allies co-vote more with more connection) cannot be tested with these data because there is almost no variation among same-coalition dyads.
key_findings.numbers: Of 594 same-coalition dyads, 574 (97%) voted together 100% of the time on the forty Environment Committee bills.

key_findings.finding: Co-voting distribution is bimodal: about one-third of all pairs vote together 100% of the time, and the authors therefore drop unanimous observations in the log-odds model.
key_findings.numbers: 1,920 observations; 594 pairs at 100% co-voting; only five pairs at 0%.

key_findings.finding: Connectivity structure: contact is sparse and many pairs are poorly connected, though the measure has a meaningful spread.
key_findings.numbers: Density 5.7% (9.7% symmetric; 6.1% on 118 of 1,920 possible ties). Mean point connectivity 2.2, median 2, maximum 12 (one Spanish EPP and British Conservative pair). 12.4% of dyads have zero connectivity. 39.5% of office pairs are cut off by removing one node.

key_findings.finding: Response bias tests show no evident bias by region or EU accession date, but the authors stress that network data require caution below 100% response.
key_findings.numbers: Region: Pearson chi-square 0.935, p = 0.817 (N = 65). Accession date: chi-square 0.3752, p = 0.540. Response 32 of 65 offices (47%).

key_findings.finding: Theory and method contribution: the authors argue voting interdependence must be modelled at the dyad level with network dependence handled explicitly; the conditional relationship with ideology is central.

limitations: Small network: 32 of 65 offices responded (47%), and the authors say non-response is assumed missing at random (p. 614). A 47% response rate means the network needs caution, and the authors say results below 100% response are less certain (p. 616).
The data are restricted to one committee and one policy area (environment and consumer protection) for one term (p. 613). The authors say generalization is limited (p. 627).

Causality is not resolved: the authors describe a simultaneous, endogenous process between ties and co-voting (pp. 610, 620, 627) and say their empirical tests are compromised by an intractable causality problem (p. 628).

Results are sensitive to specification changes (lagged votes, joint-membership instrument, reverse-causality models) (fn. 81, p. 627). The authors defend the chosen specification but do not show the alternatives.
Hypothesis 2 is not testable: nearly all same-coalition dyads vote together, leaving little variance (p. 625).

Relational measures: connectivity is based on reported contact, which is directed and then symmetrized (p. 617); the connectivity measure is sensitive to specification (fn. 72, p. 620; max-flow alternatives were tried).
The data collection is hard for social network data because staff are reluctant to reveal contacts; the authors say the survey was very specialized and precluded immediate data additions (p. 627).
Missing data and lack of variance on some key terms limit inference (p. 628). Data cannot be shared publicly because of the sensitivity of personal connections (p. 602, fn. on first page).

summary_md:
Ringe, Victor and Gross (BJPS 2013) ask whether legislators' social ties with allies and adversaries relate to how they vote. Their argument is that legislators treat colleagues as sources of cues. A tie to an adversary is useful when the two disagree, because a predictable opponent gives a reliable signal for confirming or revising one's own position.

The data come from staff-reported contacts among the 65 offices on the European Parliament's Environment Committee. The survey ran in 2007 and 32 of the 65 offices responded (47%). Votes are 40 final roll calls on committee bills from 2004 to 2008. The authors model the dyadic co-voting rate with OLS, with a linear mixed model that has crossed random effects for respondent and alter, and with a log-odds mixed model.

For pairs from opposing voting blocs, each extra unit of point connectivity goes with about 10% lower odds of voting together (95% CI 7-13%; n = 1,319 non-unanimous dyads). On the probability scale, predicted co-voting moves from 52% to 44% across ±1 SD of connectivity. Bloc membership dominates (log-odds 2.91), and party adds nothing once bloc is controlled. The allies hypothesis (H2) could not be tested, because 97% of same-bloc dyads always voted together.

The design is cross-sectional and covers one committee in one policy area, with no identification strategy. The authors report that results are sensitive to specification.

The paper matters here for three reasons:
1. Several of Paul's components read a tie, or a cross-party tie, as a positive conduit for alignment. This paper is evidence that contact between opponents is associated with disagreement, not agreement.
2. It supports conditioning network signals on bloc or party, and keeping edge sign. It does not support pooling ties without sign.
3. It shows that dyadic tests need explicit modelling of network dependence, which none of the system's dyad-level checks has.

Every effect here is an association in one EP committee, measured from reported staff contact rather than cosponsorship. It transfers to the US House cosponsorship graph only as a direction to test, not as a calibrated number.

bearings.paper_claim: Among opposing-bloc MEP dyads, higher point connectivity predicts LESS co-voting. The log-odds multilevel coefficient is -0.1020 (SE 0.0307), about -10% odds per unit (95% CI 7-13%). Predicted co-voting falls from 52% to 44% between -1 SD and +1 SD of connectivity. Window: 40 Environment Committee roll calls, 2004-2008. Denominator: 1,319 non-unanimous dyads.
bearings.system_side: cpf_diffusion gives every cross-party edge a positive contagion weight of 0.4 + 0.6*sqrt(bpf_u*bpf_v). Even non-bridge out-party pairs keep a positive floor of 0.4. build_P turns that weight into a positive activation probability for the cascade, coalition, frontier, scenario and route engines.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's tie is staff-reported informational contact, not cosponsorship. The setting is a multi-party EP committee, not the two-party US Congress, and the result is cross-sectional association with acknowledged simultaneity and sensitivity to specification (fn. 81). It does not show that cross-party diffusion is zero or negative in US cosponsorship. It only shows that a positive cross-party contagion floor is not supported by the one direct test of opponent ties in this paper. Use it to motivate a test (cross-party pair connectivity against later co-voting on CU roll calls, stratified by party pair), not to change a constant.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Cascade activation kernel build_P and partisan edge factors|Cascade activation kernel build_P and partisan edge factors]]

bearings.paper_claim: Social connection between political adversaries goes with less voting agreement, not more. The theory is that ties to adversaries carry cues one expects to disagree with, not persuasion toward the adversary's side (H1 confirmed; opposed-bloc baseline about 50% co-voting).
bearings.system_side: The BAKKER_XCUE signing passes a cross-party pro-cue through sqrt(bpf_u*bpf_v), so cues from non-bridge out-partisans fall to about 0. The value is clamped at 0, never negative, because the code comment says the backfire magnitude is not invented. Priming pressure therefore does not treat out-party ties as persuasive.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The direction agrees: out-party ties should not count as pro-pressure. The paper's negative association hints that the clamp at 0 could be conservative. However, the association is not causal, the votes are EP votes, and the tie is staff contact, so it does not justify adding a negative (backfire) term. The clamp at 0 remains the right default.

bearings.paper_claim: The link between connectivity and agreement depends on whether the pair are expected allies or adversaries (bloc). Pooling ties without that condition mixes the signs: same-bloc pairs co-vote about 100% of the time (574 of 594), while for opposed-bloc pairs more contact predicts less co-voting.
bearings.system_side: Neighbour imputation takes the unweighted mean of TSCORE over every cosponsor neighbour, with at least 5 neighbours and |est| >= 0.75, and does not condition on party. Masking validation reports 77% sign agreement but does not include a party-only baseline. The co-movement test on cosponsor ties and HCoI ties was null.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper implies that an imputation pooled across parties combines two relationships of opposite sign. The open question (does it beat a party-only baseline?) is the right test, and a split into same-party and cross-party neighbours is the natural next diagnostic. The transfer is conceptual, since the paper's outcome is votes and not stance labels. The 77% figure stays UNVERIFIED as a network effect until it is compared with a party-only baseline (DE-062).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation|Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation]]

bearings.paper_claim: Unsigned contact is not alignment. Between adversaries, more contact is associated with less agreement (about -10% odds of co-voting per connectivity unit, opposed-bloc dyads, EP Environment Committee 2004-2008). The authors infer the tie's meaning (ally or adversary) from bloc, not from the contact itself.
bearings.system_side: The co-appearance layer records unsigned, undirected pairs, with a 'bipartisan' boolean for cross-party pairs (1,151 pairs). The member-reference layer keeps LLM valence per context window as net = (pos - neg)/scored. Both layers are display-only.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This supports keeping the reference layer signed. It also warns against reading a cross-party co-appearance count as closeness or alignment: under D-025 these are heuristic layer outputs, not closeness. A broadcast pairing of opponents may be adversarial (a debate format). The test the component itself proposes (does negative sign predict lower future cosponsorship?) is the analogue of the paper's H1 and should be run with party-pair strata. The settings differ (EP staff contact vs US media co-appearance), so the evidence is weak.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-sna#Co-appearance and signed member-reference layers (display only)|Co-appearance and signed member-reference layers (display only)]]

bearings.paper_claim: The authors measure actual staff-reported contacts instead of proxies such as cosponsorship, and argue this raises confidence that the measure captures information exchange. Reported contact was sparse: density 5.7% (6.1%, 118 of 1,920 possible directed ties), mean point connectivity 2.2, and 12.4% of dyads at zero.
bearings.system_side: The cosponsor graph is the default substrate for cascades, routes and imputation. It assumes cosponsorship is an influence and alignment tie (original 1.0, regular 0.5; mean-symmetrized).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper does not test cosponsorship, so it cannot say cosponsor edges are wrong. It shows that a measured contact tie and agreement can diverge when the pair are adversaries, which bears on the 'alignment tie' assumption for cross-party cosponsor edges. It does not argue for dropping regular cosponsor edges or for per-edge volume normalization, both of which were measured and rejected here. Do not read it that way.

gaps_exposed: No dyad-level test in the system models network dependence, such as crossed random effects for both members of a dyad, or QAP and ERGM approaches. This applies to the co-movement tests in stance_dynamics.py, to any future test of whether negative references predict lower cosponsorship, and to cross-party diffusion checks. The paper shows that dyads sharing a member are not independent.

No component conditions the meaning of a tie on whether the pair are expected allies or adversaries (bloc or party pair) before using it as alignment evidence. Neighbour imputation and the 0.4 cross-party diffusion floor both pool or attenuate ties without sign.

No layer treats ties to opponents as information channels, that is, cue-taking from a predictable adversary that confirms one's own position. The system models cross-party ties only as attenuated positive contagion or as zero pressure.

There is no external test of the cross-party sign in the cascade kernel. Neither direction of the cross-party term (positive diffusion at 0.4 + 0.6*sqrt(bpf)) has been checked against US co-voting or cosponsorship outcomes, stratified by party pair.
flags: The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). Its preference for measured contact over cosponsorship proxies must NOT be read as support for dropping cosponsor edges.

The point-connectivity coefficients are heuristic association measures from one EP committee. Under D-025 they must not be restated as closeness, access or introduction probabilities, and influence language should not be used.

The -10% odds figure is a stratum result (opposed-bloc pairs, 1,319 non-unanimous dyads, 40 roll calls 2004-2008). It must not be quoted as a pooled tie effect. The same-bloc hypothesis (H2) was untestable (574 of 594 same-bloc dyads at 100%), so the paper gives no evidence on ties among allies.
The authors report sensitivity to specification (fn. 81) and an unresolved simultaneity problem. Any system use stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it on US data (DE-062).
Paul's position for melange-sna.co-appearance-and-references lists this paper as 'on disk, ink only'. It has now been read in full, so that note is stale.
paul_alignment: Paul's highlights centre on the mechanism. Voting is interdependent, ties are strategic choices about information, and adversaries supply cues that update beliefs. He also highlighted the method (multilevel models with crossed random effects for dependence), the use of staff networks as a proxy for office networks, and the headline H1 result. The evidence matches his reading. However, the system has absorbed little of it. Cross-party ties appear only as attenuated positive contagion (cpf_diffusion) or as zero priming pressure (Bakker clamp). No layer uses adversary ties as information channels, and no dyadic test models dependence the way he highlighted. His only listed position cites the paper under co-appearance-and-references as 'ink only'. That is stale: the full paper's main transfer is a caution that unsigned contact is not alignment, plus support for keeping the reference layer signed and stratifying by party pair. The highlight on staff as extensions of their legislators fits the staffer-network premise. But the staff ties in this paper are reported contacts, not concurrent payroll overlap, so it does not validate the overlap edge rule.

related.why: This is the same lead author's co-voting network centrality work on the European Parliament. It uses the same co-voting outcome, but as a centrality measure where this paper uses it as a dyadic outcome.

This paper finds that bloc, not party, carries the co-voting signal, and that cross-bloc ties have the opposite sign. That parallels Aref and Neal's signed-network coalitions beyond party labels, which the system's signed_coalitions.py implements.
Bakker reports that out-party cues do not persuade. This paper finds that adversary contact goes with less agreement. Together they ground the lt_priming clamp on cross-party cues.
Both papers model legislative behaviour as cue-taking from information sources, one from interest-group letters and one from colleague ties.
Sotoudeh builds influence on cosponsorship ties. This paper argues for measured contact over cosponsorship proxies and shows that ties to adversaries go with less agreement.
Both argue that the sign or type of a relationship changes what a tie predicts, which is the issue behind the system's signed member-reference layer.
Both papers frame social network analysis as the study of information exchange through reported ties.

extraction.document_type: Conference paper (UAI 2021), arXiv preprint v1; algorithm paper with simulation experiments
extraction.coverage: Full text read in chunks (all 1341 extracted lines: front matter, abstract, introduction, related work, problem setup, MDP formulation, RL4IM algorithm, state abstraction, reward shaping and theorems, experiments, conclusion, references). Paul's annotation file was read in full: 35 highlight items on pages 1-4, none with note text. Figures 1-5 are covered through captions and axis labels only, since plotted values are not in the extracted text. Lobbying, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislators, text measurement and path-finding are absent from the paper. Network content is seed selection for influence spread. Allocation appears only as a per-round budget of B seeds over T rounds, not economic allocation. Highlight colors vary (yellow, green, blue, pink) and the file has no legend.
extraction.research_question: How to choose seed nodes for influence maximization when each invited node is only probabilistically willing to accept (contingency-aware IM), at low computational cost on new social networks, using reinforcement learning that generalizes to unseen networks without re-running an expensive greedy algorithm (Abstract p.1; Introduction p.1-2).
extraction.theory: Influence spreads under the Independent Cascade (IC) model (Goldenberg et al. 2001; Kempe et al. 2003), Sec 3.1 p.3. Seed willingness is Bernoulli with a known probability q, Sec 3.1 p.3. The influence function is treated as submodular (stated as "usually submodular", Sec 4.3 p.4). The sequential decision is a discrete-time MDP with sub-steps (t,b), Sec 3.2 p.3-4. The learner is DQN with structure2vec-style graph embeddings (Khalil et al. 2017), Sec 4.1 p.4. The key derived result is a surrogate reward (Eq. 11, Theorem 1, p.4) under assumptions Eqs. 9-10 (marginal contribution depends only on the count of willing predecessors; arithmetic-sequence form).
extraction.data: Synthetic graphs only. Power-law graphs from a Barabasi-Albert growth model with an extra triangle step (Onnela et al. 2007): average degree 3, triangle probability 0.05, Sec 5.1 p.5. Unit of observation: graph and seed node. One real-scale runtime reference: CHANGE on a 1000-node, 4974-edge network, propagation probability 0.2, sampling frequency 50, one Intel i9-9820X core; runtime reaches about 10 hours at 20 seeds (Figure 1, p.1-2). extraction.method: Reinforcement learning for influence maximization (RL4IM), Sec 4, p.4-5. (1) Each sub-step selects one node; the state is a 3 x |V| binary matrix (unselected; selected-willing; selected-unwilling; selected-unknown) plus fixed graph G, Sec 3.2 p.3-4. (2) State abstraction: X_bar = X1 + q*X3 (Eq. 5, Sec 4.2 p.4), with a feasible-action set maintained separately for unwilling nodes. (3) Reward shaping: the exact expected marginal reward (Eq. 6) is replaced by r~ = (1-q)*dI0 + q*dI_{b-1} (Eq. 11, Theorem 1), where dI0 and dI_{b-1} bound the marginal contribution (Lemma 1, Eq. 8). Theorem 2: reward computation falls from O(2^b) to O(1). Theorem 3 gives the gap bound max{(q-(1-q)^{b-1})(dI0-dI_{b-1}), (1-q-q^{b-1})(dI0-dI_{b-1})}. (4) Training: DQN with experience replay (memory 4096, batch 32, max 2000 training steps, discount 0.99, S2V embedding + 128-unit MLP, Adam), Sec 5.1 p.5. Baselines: CHANGE greedy (Wilder et al. 2018), S2V-DQN-IM (state abstraction added; reward uses dI_{b-1}), and Random. Validation uses 20 episodes x 5 graphs per checkpoint; IM spread is simulated 100 times per estimate.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. This is an algorithm and simulation study with no quasi-experimental or observational identification. Performance is measured on held-out synthetic graphs: validation graphs select hyperparameters and checkpoints, and unseen test graphs measure generalization. Theorem 3 bounds the approximation gap of the surrogate reward under Eqs. 9-10, which are stated assumptions, not identified facts.
extraction.scope: Population: synthetic power-law social networks, with a real-scale runtime illustration only (Figure 1). Institutions: Harvard Center for Research on Computation and Society; Nanyang Technological University (p.1). Era: arXiv June 2021, UAI 2021. Application framing: low-resource non-profits running HIV-prevention peer-leader interventions among homeless youth (Introduction p.1-2; Section 3 p.3). Generalization is claimed only across synthetic graphs with similar characteristics (Introduction p.2).

summary_md:
Chen, Qiu, Ou, An and Tambe (UAI 2021) study contingency-aware influence maximization. In this setting an invited seed accepts only with a probability q, which is known in advance and the same for every node. Seeds are chosen over T rounds of B seeds, and willingness is revealed only at the end of each round. The authors cast the problem as an MDP and train a DQN with structure2vec embeddings (RL4IM). Two devices make training tractable: a state abstraction (X1 + q*X3) and a surrogate reward, (1-q)*dI0 + q*dI_{b-1}. The surrogate cuts reward computation from O(2^b) to O(1), and Theorem 3 bounds its gap from the exact reward, though the bound becomes arbitrarily loose as q approaches 0 or 1. All experiments use synthetic Barabasi-Albert-type graphs: 200 nodes, Independent Cascade with p=0.1, q=0.6, budget 8, and 200 runs per setting. On these graphs RL4IM matches or slightly beats the CHANGE greedy baseline, and both reach roughly twice Random. The paper's case for RL is runtime on new, unseen networks: CHANGE takes about 10 hours at 20 seeds on a 1,000-node graph. It gives no empirical estimate of q for any real population.

For Melange the paper is the cited source of the SGATE contingency gate (fec/moneyball_core.py:626-630). The gate is used non-adaptively in the coalition and frontier spread estimators. The system goes beyond the paper's model in three ways: q varies by member (seed_prob x stance gate), there is a single round with no observed willingness, and committed allies are never gated. The paper's theorems do not cover that model, and the system does not need them, because it estimates expected spread directly by Monte Carlo. The paper does not validate any take-up rate. The 0.60 baseline in seed_prob equals the paper's arbitrary simulation default. The planned H1 test correlates seed_prob with unconditional new cosponsorships, which is not the conditional-on-invitation quantity the paper models. The runtime argument for RL does not apply to a fixed 533-member chamber graph. All agent analysis here is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

Source: Paul's addendum "Melange Annotated Bibliography — Addendum" (sha12 d09295bf5960), read in full (68 lines). The companion reviewer-annotation file _annots/d09295bf5960.json does not exist, so there are no reviewer comments or highlights to add. Entries are Paul's own annotations paraphrased, and citations are recorded as he wrote them; I did not verify them externally.

Overarching argument: the section extends the static influence-maximization entries (Kempe et al. 2003; Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher 1978, covered elsewhere) into a dynamic regime organized in three tiers that mirror the Melange architecture. Tier 1 is one-shot greedy, which is static and submodular and gives the 1-1/e (about 63%) bound. Tier 2 is adaptive greedy, the bridge: a subordinate routine that replans within a campaign as intelligence arrives, with a survival guarantee (Golovin-Krause; CELF makes it computationally practical). Tier 3 is the RL envelope, where a learned outer policy handles cross-campaign compounding, where no greedy guarantee reaches.

Unifying claim: the inner static problem is submodular, the inner sequential problem is adaptive submodular, and the full cross-campaign problem is non-submodular. Paul asserts that RL4CCIM confirms the last point for complex contagion, and that the non-submodular regime is where the durable competitive moat lives.

Systems linked: the operational layer (D* Lite / LPA*, incremental replanning) maps to adaptive submodularity; the strategic layer (MCTS and the orienteering "reach-while-collecting" frame) maps to the RL-IM sequential, long-horizon problem; the political-capital budget maps to GCOMB's budget constraint; the subordinate greedy routine feeds the outer MDP through marginal-influence shaping rewards.

Research questions and implicit hypotheses: (a) whether coalition formation in Congress is a complex contagion (a fence-sitter commits only once enough allies have), which Paul calls "plausibly" true and which would place Melange outside the submodular regime; (b) whether relationship and persuasion costs, unknown a priori, can be learned by probing (Kamarthi); (c) whether lobbying commitment that is probabilistic rather than guaranteed (Chen 2021) changes the seeding policy.

Stated gaps and caveats in the addendum: adaptive submodularity presumes exact expected spread, which is NP-hard in general, and this is the stated reason Paul still drifts toward learned methods. The frontier paragraph says the four anchored RL entries are "sufficient"; the section in fact anchors seven RL-IM entries plus foundations, so that sentence is loosely worded. The frontier work (MaDGNN) is named without authors or DOI and is not anchored. The Golovin entry's "first to study influence maximization under the adaptive model" is Paul's priority claim and is unverified here.

The sidecar C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\b0774147a262.json does not exist, so there are no reviewer comments or highlights to fold in. The document lists 8 cited works. Only 4 (Birkenmaier and Lechner; Kim et al.; Peng et al.; Ramey et al.) have annotation text. The other 4 (Alkazzi and Okumura; Joo and Steinert-Threlkeld; Taherdoost and Madanchian; Steinert-Threlkeld) are citation-only.

Overarching argument: Paul treats machine learning and NLP applied to public political text (congressional floor speech, public statements, lobbying filings) as a way to produce actor-level attributes (personality traits, policy positions, emotion) that can be placed on nodes of a social-network-analysis graph. The purpose he names is political intelligence: lobbying strategy, industry alignment, and how to pitch policy to a specific member of Congress.

Research questions and gaps Paul states:
1. Conversion step. Birkenmaier and Lechner, Peng et al., and Ramey et al. each say the pipeline does not specify how a model's output becomes a graph node or vector. This is the most repeated gap in the document.
2. Ambiguity. Birkenmaier and Lechner say the method does not separate ambiguous statements.
3. Conflict. Kim et al. do not show inter-industry conflict over a specific bill, which Paul says matters for political intelligence.
4. Temporal lag. Kim et al. are reactive, not predictive, because filing reports lag current positions.
5. Model limits. Peng et al. say long-distance dependency is the main obstacle for most emotion models; stacking reduces but does not remove it.
6. Venue coverage. Ramey et al. offer no pipeline for textual venues beyond their own, and Paul says a framework for contextual or auditory constraints is also needed.

Synthesis: Birkenmaier and Lechner and Ramey et al. both concern personality measurement from speech or text, with Ramey et al. as the older foundation and Birkenmaier and Lechner as the newer, codebook-backed method. Kim et al. and Birkenmaier and Lechner both concern the actor-to-graph link. Peng et al. supplies the model landscape that the other two would run on.

Self-declared gap: Paul says his own technical grounding is not yet sufficient for Peng et al. and plans a second reading after more background.

bearings.paper_claim: Contingency-aware IM: a selected seed is willing only with a Bernoulli probability q, which is known a priori and identical across nodes (Sec 3.1, footnote 2). Experiments use q=0.6 by default and test q=0.2 and 0.8. No real-world value of q is estimated.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 3.1 p.3 (footnote 2); Sec 5.1 p.5; Q3 Fig 5(a) p.6
bearings.system_side: gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob(n) x SGATE[tier]). SGATE runs from Highly Persuadable 1.00 down to Opponent 0.35, with unknown at 0.85. The effective take-up prior therefore spans 0.15 to 0.90 and differs by member. Ally, Champion and Defender are set to 1.0, and in the spread estimators the pro core is unconditional rather than gated. seed_prob = clip(0.60 + .10 coop + .06 breadth + .04 visibility, 0.30, 0.90). Its 0.60 baseline equals the paper's simulation default q, which was chosen for the simulation and is not an estimate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the modeling idea transfers: invitation is not activation. The paper's q is homogeneous and its analysis is multi-round. SGATE is heterogeneous, graded by stance and personality, and used single-shot, so Theorems 1-3 do not cover it. The paper gives no evidence for any SGATE level or for the 0.60 baseline. The source population is HIV peer leaders among homeless youth, not legislators. Until H1 or a contact log measures take-up, SGATE values remain owner design priors.

bearings.paper_claim: Modeling unwillingness inside the objective, rather than reacting to realized willingness, is the authors' explanation for RL4IM matching or slightly beating greedy CHANGE. At T=1 (single round, T x B = 8) RL4IM and CHANGE remain the two best methods, and both reach roughly twice Random. All results come from synthetic power-law graphs under IC with p=0.1.
bearings.paper_location: Q3-Q4, Sec 5.2 p.6; paragraph after Q5 p.6; Fig 5(a)-(b)
bearings.system_side: Lazy greedy up to 60 seeds. spread() draws each lobbied seed's activation against gate(n,cs) on a dedicated CRN stream at key offset 2^62 (lines 126-128), so the expectation over willingness sits inside the greedy objective. A failed contest activation leaves the target an opponent (lines 129-131). This is non-adaptive single-round contingency-aware IM on an IC-type competitive cascade.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This supports the design choice of putting take-up uncertainty into the expected-spread objective. It does not validate the cascade kernel, the gate values or the two-colour competition; the paper models a single colour only. The evidence is synthetic graphs at about 200 nodes, which is comparable in scale to the 533-member graph, but there are no political data. The 'slightly better' edge is reported qualitatively, with no numbers.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-allocation#Budget frontier with knee and electoral modes|Budget frontier with knee and electoral modes]]

bearings.paper_claim: Under contingency, the exact expected marginal contribution of a seed depends on which earlier seeds turned out willing (O(2^b) cases). Influence is assumed submodular (Eq. 7).
bearings.system_side: The coalition allocator computes each candidate's individual marginal spread({n}) - base with the seed gate inside the MC loop. It then water-fills the budget on those individual marginals and reports the honest joint spread of the funded set, because summing individual marginals overstates the joint gain (M2 fix).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's O(2^b) dependence on earlier seeds' willingness is the same non-additivity that the joint-spread report exposes. Allocating on single-seed marginals ignores that dependence. The paper's surrogate reward is one cheap correction, but it needs a homogeneous q and its Eqs. 9-10 assumptions, so it would not port directly to heterogeneous gates. This is a diagnostic allocator, so the stakes are low.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-allocation#Per-topic flip and coalition allocators|Per-topic flip and coalition allocators]]

bearings.paper_claim: q is the probability that a node is willing when it is selected or invited. It is a conditional take-up rate that the paper assumes known a priori.
bearings.system_side: H1 ('seeding, Chen/SNAM') tests Spearman(frozen seed_prob, NEW cosponsorships after the freeze) over all covered members. Engaged-only scoring is unavailable until receipted contact data exists. The F5 replay found 72 of 511 new-event members against a 150-member floor, so H1 is UNDERPOWERED and its look is unspent.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Unconditional new cosponsorship mixes the take-up rate with who gets contacted and with base activity. Chen's q is defined conditional on an invitation. A pass on unconditional H1 would therefore not validate seed_prob as a contingency probability, and a miss would not refute it. The construct match needs the engaged-only arm, that is, a contact log.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-validation#Prospective receptivity contract (H1-H2) and forecast ledger|Prospective receptivity contract (H1-H2) and forecast ledger]]

gaps_exposed: The system never observes or updates willingness. The paper's setting is multi-round: willingness is revealed at the end of each round and later seeds are chosen knowing it. Melange seeding is a one-shot plan. Replanning after observed take-up would need an outreach or contact log, which does not exist.
No empirical take-up rate backs either SGATE or seed_prob. The paper supplies none for any population, and the 0.60 baseline equals its arbitrary simulation default.
The H1 receptivity contract measures unconditional cosponsorship, not take-up conditional on contact. The construct Chen defines cannot be tested until receipted contact data exists.

The paper shows that a seed's marginal value depends on earlier seeds' realized willingness. The coalition allocator funds on individual gated marginals and only reports the joint shortfall afterwards. It does not fund on conditional marginals.
flags: Language: seed_prob x SGATE is a heuristic design prior. Do not describe it as a measured take-up, access or commitment probability for a legislator. The paper validates no q for any real population, and H1 is unspent and underpowered (72/511 against a 150 floor).

Paul's addendum files Chen 2021 under 'C. RL influence maximization - the non-submodular envelope'. The paper explicitly assumes submodularity (Eq. 7) and IC. The non-submodular, complex-contagion work is the same group's RL4CCIM (chen-nd-complex-contagion-influence). Chen 2021 should not be cited as evidence for the non-submodular tier.

Paul's takeaway describes the method as 'observe-then-act'. That is accurate only between rounds; within a round willingness is unknown and is replaced by its expectation (X1 + q*X3). The system as built observes nothing (single-shot), so the 'observe-then-act' framing describes an unbuilt capability.

The paper's motivation for RL (repeated recomputation on new graphs by low-compute NGOs) does not apply to Melange's fixed 533-member chamber graphs. Its quality result is parity with greedy. Neither supports replacing the CELF or lazy-greedy layer with a learned policy.
No rule conflicts. The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, and it uses no LDA or reciprocity claims.
paul_alignment: Paul's mapping is right in substance and is already built as SGATE. His mapping: a lobbied legislator may or may not take up an invitation, so contact is not activation. The receptivity docstring echoes it ('legislators know they are being lobbied'). The gate is applied inside the frontier and coalition spread estimators. Two parts of his note are stale or loose relative to the system and the paper. First, 'sequential, observe-then-act seeding' describes the paper's multi-round setting, but Melange seeds single-shot and never observes willingness, so that half of his takeaway is an extension, not current behaviour. Second, he files the paper in the non-submodular RL tier, but Chen 2021 assumes submodularity; the complex-contagion argument belongs to RL4CCIM. His broader expectation that a learned policy (GCOMB, RL) will replace greedy is not supported here. RL4IM only matches greedy, and its advantage is runtime on new graphs, which Melange does not face.

related.why: Same group (Chen, Tambe). It carries the RL-for-IM framing into complex contagion, which is the non-submodular regime that Paul's addendum attributes to this paper.

The paper contrasts itself with adaptive submodularity, which it says does not address uncertainty in node willingness. Golovin-Krause is the operational-layer bound the joint optimizer uses as a diagnostic.
Cited as RL for IM under graph-exploration uncertainty. It sits beside Chen as the other learned-policy entry in Paul's sequential-IM addendum.
SNAM behaviour-aware IM survey, cited together with Chen as 'Chen/SNAM' for seed_prob in receptivity_layer.py and outcome_contract.py H1.
Source of the competitive IC cascade into which the system inserts Chen's contingency gate. Chen models a single colour only.
Graph-embedding or GNN-based influence maximization: learned node representations for seed selection, as in RL4IM's structure2vec backbone.
Deep-RL influence maximization in the same S2V or DQN lineage, applied to edge activation instead of contingent seeds.
Questions whether greedy is needed at all. Read with Chen's parity-with-greedy result, it suggests learned or heuristic policies buy runtime, not quality, at Melange's scale.

backlinks.why: Chen et al. relax Trivedi's assumption that seeds always activate. The system's seed gate (SGATE x seed_prob) implements that contingency, which the plain DHICM/CELF comparison ignores.
Contingency-aware seeding, the basis of SGATE, is the adaptive-feedback setting that Golovin-Krause Thm 5/6 analyze, with independent take-up failures.
Chen's contingency-aware seeding (SGATE) and Cai's partial zealotry both model agents who resist adoption. Cai finds such agents receive fewer resources.

Both use reinforcement learning to replace a hand-set rule policy. Chen et al. do it for seeding legislators-as-nodes under take-up uncertainty, which is the literature actually behind the SGATE seed gate. Zeng applies RL only to physical swarm control.
Both make contact conditional on the target's receptivity. Chen does it as contingency-aware seeding, which the system implements as SGATE; this paper does it as credibility-gated contact.

summary_md:
Khan et al. (2025) built a Roman Urdu dataset of Pakistani political tweet-and-reply pairs, about 8,374 labelled agree, disagree or unrelated. They benchmarked five TF-IDF classifiers against a fine-tuned RoBERTa. Reported accuracy: random forest 0.95, SVM 0.94, logistic regression 0.93, decision tree 0.92, naive bayes 0.89, all on 1,675 test rows. RoBERTa reached 0.97, but on an "augmented" set with support 6,699, so it was not scored on the same test split as the others. There is one 80/20 split, with no kappa, no seeds, no hyperparameters and no confidence intervals. The augmentation is described with image operations (rotation, flipping), and the conclusion contradicts the results section. As evidence the paper is weak. The ranking gaps of 1 to 4 points have no error bars, and the transformer-wins headline is not a like-for-like comparison.

It still matters here because the system cites it as a method source. fec/stance/train_stance_domain.py is literally titled "Khan et al. pipeline". It copies the paired target-conditioned input, the five-classifier ladder, the class-balancing analog and the expectation that "transformer should beat all". fec/stance/stance_eval.py takes macro-F1 as its headline and adds "unrelated" as a class "per ICCK/TACS" practice. On Paul's own data the paper's two transferable claims did not hold. A transformer on the augmented press set scored 0.757 macro-F1, below a tuned word+char LinearSVC at 0.816. The Khan multi-view augmentation hurt the classical models and was rejected on 2026-07-03. The lasting value is in the evaluation conventions: "unrelated" as its own class, macro-F1 as the headline, and fine-tuning only once labels are clean. The model-ranking claims do not carry over. The code docstring repeats the paper's 0.93 to 0.97 figures as if they were faithful, comparable numbers. It should flag that RoBERTa was scored on a different test set.

bearings.paper_claim: Classical models on TF-IDF features rank RF 0.95 > SVM 0.94 > LR 0.93 > DT 0.92 > NB 0.89 (test n=1,675). Fine-tuned RoBERTa with tweet+comment paired input reaches 0.97 (support 6,699, augmented set). Augmentation and class balancing are credited with gains, but no with/without comparison is given.
bearings.system_side: train_stance_domain.py declares itself the Khan pipeline adapted to the CU domain. It builds a target-conditioned paired input ('target: X. speaker: Y. span + text'), runs the same five classifiers with class_weight='balanced', has an --augment flag that adds multi-view rows (title view and stance-span view, oppose rows upsampled) to TRAIN only, and has a --transformer path (distilroberta, 4 epochs, inverse-frequency loss weights).
bearings.code_ref: fec/stance/train_stance_domain.py:3-13 (docstring cites the paper and restates its accuracies), :31-34 (paired input), :42-59 (Khan multi-view augmentation), :94-103 (five-model ladder; prints 'Khan et al. ordering ... transformer should beat all'), :120-127 (class-weighted RoBERTa loss)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper had about 8k labels in one language and one domain, a single split, and RoBERTa scored on a different and larger test set. The system has 456 train / 87 test press rows with a never-reshuffled split. The mechanics transfer (paired input, balanced loss). The model ordering and the augmentation benefit do not: neither is tested like-for-like in the paper, and both failed here.

bearings.paper_claim: The transformer beats every classical model (0.97 vs at most 0.95), and dataset augmentation and balancing improve performance.
bearings.paper_location: Section 4.4.2 p.92; Section 4.5 p.93; Abstract p.78
bearings.system_side: On the CU press gold set, the transformer trained on augmented data reached 0.757 macro-F1, below the tuned word+char LinearSVC at 0.816 (83.9% acc, untouched test n=87). Brain note 2026-07-02 says augmenting the same 456 rows cannot close the gap; new labels are needed. On 2026-07-03, 'Khan augmentation HURTS classical (rejected)'. Production is the SVM, not a transformer.

They show that the paper's ordering does not carry to small English congressional press corpora. The paper's own comparison is also confounded (different test supports), so neither result settles the general question.

bearings.paper_claim: Stance is a three-way task in which 'unrelated' is a first-class label alongside agree and disagree. The paper reports per-class precision, recall and F1 with macro averages.
bearings.system_side: The S1 evaluation harness scores any prediction column against adjudicated gold, with macro-F1 as the headline 'per ICCK/TACS.2025.928069 practice'. Its class set includes 'unrelated'. The tweet trainer uses the same four classes, and its headline is 5-fold CV rather than one split.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This transfers fully. Labelling and metric conventions do not depend on language or domain. The system goes further than the paper by using CV for small n and slice breakdowns. The paper itself gives no CV, no agreement statistic and no CI, so it is a source for the convention only, not for validation rigor.

bearings.paper_claim: A fine-tuned RoBERTa reaches 0.97 accuracy on political stance, with errors concentrated in sarcastic, ambiguous and implicit statements, and implicit disagreement mislabelled as unrelated.
bearings.system_side: The production transformer reader is Political DEBATE NLI, fine-tuned on 552 rows for 3 epochs. It scores 0.839 acc / kappa 0.742 held out and 0.571 on the adversarial goldeval frame. A tuned SVM ties it (0.835 macro-F1). The recorded dominant error is implicit support read as neutral (n=78).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The 0.97 headline should not be used as a target or prior. It comes from about 8k in-domain labels and a non-common test set. The error-mode finding (implicit and indirect stance) does transfer, and it matches the system's neutral/support seam. Treat the paper as weak, qualitative support only.

gaps_exposed: The paper's one usable pointer is that implicit and indirect stance is the residual failure. The system knows its dominant error (implicit support read as neutral, n=78), but it has no dedicated handling for implicit stance or sarcasm in either the SVM or DEBATE readers.

The production press classifier (stance_clf_composed.pkl) still has no 'unrelated' class (07-03 note), although the evaluation harness and tweet trainer treat 'unrelated' as first-class. Training and evaluation label spaces are mismatched on the press side.

train_stance_domain.py lists the paper's accuracies as a faithful baseline and expects 'transformer should beat all'. The docstring does not record that the paper scored RoBERTa on a different test support (6,699 vs 1,675), or that the system's own result reversed the ordering. A reader of the code would inherit an unsupported expectation.
flags: The code comment at fec/stance/train_stance_domain.py:103 ('transformer should beat all') and the docstring at :5-8 present the paper's model ordering as established. The paper's RoBERTa and classical results come from different test sets, and the system measured the opposite (0.757 vs 0.816 macro-F1). This is a stale or unsupported expectation embedded in code, not a validated prior.

Brain notes conflict on the augmentation history. The 2026-07-02 note credits '--augment (Khan multi-view)' plus tuning with the 83.9% / 0.816 result. The 2026-07-03 note says Khan augmentation hurts classical models and was rejected, with tune-only reaching 0.835. The component description follows the 07-03 version. Any citation of the 0.816 figure should state which configuration produced it.

Any quote of the paper's 0.97 must name its denominator: support 6,699 on the 'augmented dataset', not the 1,675-row test used for the classical models. The paper's own 'close to random guessing' claim for naive bayes at 0.89 is false against a majority-class share of about 0.36.
paul_alignment: Paul's annotated position, from Birkenmaier and Kim J. 2025, favours transformers and LLMs over bag-of-words SVMs. His highlights call SVM baselines outdated. This paper looks as if it supports that view, but its comparison is confounded, and the system's own measurements on CU press data (552 labels) went the other way. A tuned word+char LinearSVC tied or beat the fine-tuned transformers: 0.816 vs 0.757 macro-F1 for distilroberta, and 0.835 vs 0.839 against DEBATE. The LLM and API readers did beat the classical model on tweets (Opus 0.662 vs transfer 0.357 F1). So Paul's preference holds for large LLMs, not for small fine-tuned encoders on a few hundred labels. His notes do not record that outcome, and on this point they are stale relative to the system. His flagged weakness, ambiguous statements, matches the paper's stated error mode.

related.why: Ornstein evaluates LLMs on political text with small labelled sets. That is the regime where the system's evidence (LLM readers beat small fine-tuned encoders) diverges from Khan's large-label RoBERTa result.
Dai uses LLM-enhanced stance detection aimed at implicit and reasoning-dependent stance, which is the failure mode Khan reports but does not address.
Another lexical/classical stance-direction approach the system tried and rejected (3 good / 43 bad sign changes). Together they document why the classical-feature route was bounded in this domain.

Birkenmaier reports GPT-4o beating SVM and XLM-R with proper validation (Krippendorff alpha, macro-F1). Khan reports transformer superiority without comparable rigor. Paul's transformer preference rests on Birkenmaier, not on this paper.
Rice and Zorn's domain dictionaries are the lexical baseline lineage behind the legacy scorer. Khan's TF-IDF ladder is the supervised-classical step above it in the same stack.

backlinks.why: This paper stops at an introduction to NLP tooling for tweets. Khan et al. take political-tweet text to fine-tuned stance classification, which is the step the system's tweet-stance readers actually depend on.
Both infer stance from political tweets. Khan compares text classifiers on single tweets; this paper infers user-level stance from the graph with minimal text supervision.
This is the direct empirical comparison the review lacks: fine-tuned RoBERTa against traditional ML for stance in political tweets. It bears on the DEBATE-versus-LinearSVC question.
Compares fine-tuned RoBERTa with traditional ML on political-tweet stance, the same classical-versus-transformer comparison applied to the stance task the system actually runs.
Fine-tuned RoBERTa beats traditional feature-based models on political stance, which argues against dictionary and bag-of-words scoring of the kind this paper defends as efficient.

summary_md:
Taherdoost and Madanchian (2023) is a scoping review, not an empirical study. They searched Scopus for 2012-2022 journal papers that combine AI or machine learning with sentiment analysis and business or competitive terms. Of 133 hits, 43 papers were kept; the text also says 90 were examined and never reconciles the two counts. The review counts papers by year, subject, keyword, author country and citations. Its narrative section repeats claims from the papers it cites. The one useful methodological point is borrowed from Alantari et al. (2022): neural-network classifiers predict best but diagnose poorly, and topic models do the reverse. The review runs no accuracy tests of its own. It does not separate sentiment from stance or address target-dependent valence. It does not cover political text, and it describes no quality appraisal or dual screening.

For the system as built, its bearing is thin. The CU stance stack already does what the review recommends, in a stricter form. stage5_debate.py uses a fine-tuned transformer NLI reader for direction, validated on held-out human gold: 0.839, kappa 0.742, n=87, member-grouped. Lexicoder LSD2015 is kept only as a tone-intensity term (stage5_lsd.R; run_stage5.R:141-143) and never decides direction. The predictive-versus-diagnostic split gives a framing for that division: the neural reader handles prediction and the transparent dictionary handles interpretable intensity. But that rests on consumer-review evidence and one cited study. The review says nothing about the system's real bottleneck, the valence hop at 0.689 in the two-hop decomposition, or about adversarial and sign-flip targets (0.571 on goldeval). Treat it as background, not as evidence for any component's design or constants.

paul_entries.citation: Taherdoost & Madanchian 2023, Computers 12(2):37 AI and sentiment analysis

bearings.paper_claim: The paper asserts that AI understands the tone of a statement rather than just recognising words. Citing Alantari et al. 2022, it says neural-network ML gives the most accurate predictions of the text-based methods compared. The review reports no accuracy figures of its own, and its corpus is 43 business and competitive-research papers from 2012-2022.
bearings.system_side: A fine-tuned Political DEBATE NLI model (mlburnham/Political_DEBATE_base_v1.0) gives the CU stance direction. stance_sign is support, oppose or neutral, and the code states that this is independent of LSD tone. On held-out human gold it scored 0.839 accuracy / kappa 0.742 (n=87). It scored 0.796 on the 760-row frame and 0.571 on the adversarial goldeval frame.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The cited evidence covers consumer reviews and business social media, not congressional press releases. It also concerns sentiment polarity, not target-specific stance toward CU policy interests. It neither supports nor tests the system's validated accuracy, which comes from a stricter protocol (held-out, member-grouped human gold).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Fine-tuned Political DEBATE NLI stance reader|Fine-tuned Political DEBATE NLI stance reader]]

bearings.paper_claim: Alantari et al., as summarised by the review, find a trade-off: neural networks predict well but diagnose poorly, while more transparent methods are poorer predictors. The review frames word-matching approaches as the baseline that AI improves on. The trade-off is qualitative only and no numbers are given.
bearings.system_side: Lexicoder LSD2015 counts run with negation phrases removed first. They yield lsd_net_norm = net/words and lsd_charge = (pos+neg)/words. Only the magnitude (|net_norm| or charge) enters press_value = final_sign x intensity, so the dictionary sets intensity and never direction.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper agrees with the system's split of roles: an opaque predictive reader for direction and a transparent dictionary for an interpretable intensity scalar. It gives no evidence that dictionary intensity is valid on political press releases. The open question of whether LSD intensity matches human-coded intensity on this corpus is untouched. The source evidence is consumer reviews.

gaps_exposed: Neither the review nor the system validates LSD tone intensity against human-coded intensity on congressional press releases. The predictive-versus-diagnostic framing makes this gap more visible, because the dictionary is kept for interpretability, and an interpretability claim needs a validity check.

The review treats sentiment and stance as one construct and covers no target-dependent valence. The system's measured bottleneck is the valence hop (0.689 on 400 tweet golds), so the review offers nothing on the hardest part of the stack.

The review's future directions are untested suggestions: sarcasm detection, hybrid ML for sentiment categorisation, and micro-text and anaphora resolution. Anaphora and target resolution may matter for releases that name a bill only once in a roundup, which is the failure behind the rejected bill-sign override. The review offers no method or evidence for this.
flags: Paul cites Taherdoost & Madanchian 2023 as support for LLM- and transformer-based position extraction under melange-stance.debate-nli-classifier. The paper cannot carry that weight. It is a single-author scoping review with internally inconsistent counts (133 vs 90 screened; 'no documents 2012-2017' vs one 2017 paper). It reports no accuracy figures and covers no LLM or political-text evidence. Cite it as background only.

The review conflates sentiment with stance. The system's supervised-stance-stack assumes that sentiment is not stance, and stage5_debate.py:11-12 keeps the two separate. Do not cite this review for any stance-accuracy claim.

The review's only network-analysis item is Hung et al. 2020 (ref 34, a social network analysis of COVID-19 sentiment). It is not used to argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalisation, so neither rejected SNA proposal is raised. No influence or closeness wording is implied.
paul_alignment: Paul's one recorded link files this review under melange-stance.debate-nli-classifier. His takeaway there endorses LLM and transformer position extraction and flags the difficulty of ambiguous statements. The review agrees only in general direction (AI and neural nets beat word matching) and adds no evidence for that position. Kim J. 2025 and Birkenmaier & Lechner 2025 carry the actual evidence. The review does not address ambiguous statements, apart from listing sarcasm and anaphora as future work. Paul's annotation is empty (no takeaways, no anchor), so nothing he wrote is stale. The system has already moved past what the review describes: a fine-tuned NLI reader on held-out human gold, a human-label overlay, a two-hop stance-times-valence decomposition and a dictionary used for intensity only.

related.why: This is the direct empirical comparison the review lacks: fine-tuned RoBERTa against traditional ML for stance in political tweets. It bears on the DEBATE-versus-LinearSVC question.
Corpus-specific dictionaries are the evidence-based answer to the review's dismissal of word-matching methods. They also bear on whether a general LSD2015 suits congressional text.
Combines a political-communication dictionary with crowdcoding validation, the validation step that the review never addresses for dictionary tone.

The review cites a 2022 Inf Process Manag paper on social media analytics for competitive business decisions (ref 16). It appears to be the same work as this vault entry, though the first author is listed differently.
Gives the political-text LLM evidence that the review does not cover, and is relevant to Paul's LLM-extraction stance.

extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 1,131 lines of C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\266b567ac6e0.txt, including abstract, introduction, AHP/TOPSIS section, sensitivity analysis, game theory, nonlinear programming section, conclusions, references and author biographies. No Paul markup files existed ("(none)"), and the text contains no highlights or sticky-note content, so paul_markup is empty.
extraction.research_question: How can social network analysis of a single US dark money network (politically active nonprofits that take unlimited donations without disclosing donors) be made more rigorous by (a) ranking key nodes with a multi-criteria method (AHP/TOPSIS) instead of a subjective choice of centrality measure, and (b) turning the State-versus-network contest into a game with cardinal payoffs so that kinetic (prosecution/legislation) versus non-kinetic (exposure via press) strategy mixes can be solved for (Sections 1-2, 4; abstract).
extraction.data: No new sample. The unit is the organization (node) in one dark money network (DMN) that the authors analyzed in earlier unpublished work. Network-level description: a money-flow network in which ties mean funds were exchanged, node size is betweenness, tie width is dollar amount, and some nodes attended a strategy event (Figure 1, Section 1). Analytic set: the 8 organizations with the highest overall degree centrality, computed in ORA (Table 1, Section 2). Centrality values come from ORA, which lists only the top ten per metric, so some organizations have missing values (Section 4). Expert inputs: AHP pairwise judgments by the authors on Saaty's nine-point scale (criteria weights, Table 4, CR = 0.062; game payoffs, CR = 0.02244 for State and 0.03248 for DMN). No time period is stated for the network data. The number of nodes in the full DMN and the dollar amounts are not reported numerically.
extraction.method: Three linked components. (1) AHP criterion weighting over eight SNA measures (out-degree, total degree, eigenvector, betweenness, hub, in-degree, closeness, authority), with out-degree ranked first (weight 0.50199) and authority last (0.03418) (Table 2, Table 4, Section 2). (2) TOPSIS ranking of the 8 organizations on the unscaled ORA values using those weights (Table 5). Sensitivity analysis follows Alinezhad and Amini (Eq. 1): change one weight in 0.1 steps and rescale the others proportionally (Section 3). (3) Game theory on a 2x2 State (non-kinetic A vs kinetic B) by DMN (maintain centralized C vs decentralize D) game. Ordinal ranks 1-4 (Table 6) are converted to cardinal utilities by AHP (Table 7). Solutions use Nash equilibrium, mixed equalizing strategies, prudential (security-level) strategies and Nash arbitration (Feix solver; Fox lottery-alternative approach). A 5-action State vs 2-action DMN extension uses 10 strategies and a nonlinear program (Barron, Equation 2), solved in Maple 15 (Section 4).
extraction.identification: None. This is a descriptive decision-analysis and modeling paper with no causal identification strategy, no treatment or comparison group, and no estimation of effects from data. Robustness is checked only by one-weight sensitivity analysis (Section 3).
extraction.scope: Population: one US politically active dark money network of nonprofits and linked LLCs (SMLLCs), with the State modeled as the opposing player. Institutional frame: IRS rules on 501(c) political activity and disclosure, with sources cited to 2010-2014 news and IRS materials (accessed 2014-2015). The paper says the network is currently legal and that the State's kinetic options are prosecution, fines and legislation. Methodological scope is general: the authors state the method applies to any dark network. Era: circa 2010-2015 (inferred from cited sources and access dates).

limitations: The authors say explicitly that no significant changes resulted from the MADM analysis, though the findings were improved (Section 5, p. 352).

All criterion weights and game payoffs come from the authors' own subjective pairwise judgments on Saaty's scale. No external validation of weights or payoffs is reported. Sensitivity checks cover only one weight changed at a time (Section 3).

Single network, eight alternatives, unknown time period, and no reported N for the full network. Findings cannot be generalized to other dark networks without further study, although the authors state the method applies to any dark network.
ORA reports only the top ten nodes per metric, so some centrality values are missing for lower-ranked organizations (Section 4).

Kinetic and non-kinetic are defined by the authors: kinetic means IRS-related prosecution or fines, legislation on non-profit political activity, donation transparency and LLC anonymity rules; non-kinetic means press exposure of donors (Section 4, p. 348). The payoff structure depends on these definitions.

Game results depend on the assumed payoff framing. The authors state that anonymity and money flow are the DMN's main goals. The paper also includes a partisan framing of the opposing side ('Liberal leadership in the United States is unable to conduct' kinetic operations, Section 4), which is the authors' premise, not a tested finding.

The 10-strategy nonlinear solution as printed is internally inconsistent. The reported x2 = 0.92 and x4 = 0.8 sum to 1.72, not 1 as the constraint requires, and the text describes 92% and 8% shares. The likely intended value is 0.08, but this is not confirmed in the paper, so the reported solution is unverified.
Game-theory analysis treats the State and the DMN as two rational players with fixed payoffs. Structural dynamics such as DMN adaptation or donor response are not modeled.
Sources are news and advocacy reports from 2010-2014 (for example references 13, 15, 16, 18, 19), and the authors do not state dollar amounts or donor counts for the network analyzed.

summary_md:
Couch, Fox and Everton (2016) take one US dark money network: politically active nonprofits and linked single-member LLCs that pass money between them without disclosing donors. They apply two decision-analysis tools to it. First, they rank the 8 organizations with the highest degree using TOPSIS over eight ORA centrality measures. The authors set the weights themselves through AHP pairwise judgments. Out-degree gets 0.502, total degree 0.145, eigenvector 0.110 and betweenness 0.075, with a consistency ratio of 0.062. Freedom Partners Chamber of Commerce ranks first (closeness coefficient 0.754), and the ranking survives a one-weight-at-a-time sensitivity sweep. Only the top two match the plain out-degree order, and the authors admit the method produced "no significant changes". Second, they model State versus network as a 2x2 game with payoffs from AHP. The State's equalizing mix is about 85% exposure through the press and 15% prosecution or legislation. There is no outcome data, no time window and no validation, and the 10-strategy solution as printed is inconsistent (0.92 + 0.8 is not 1).

For Paul's systems the paper is mainly a caution about scope and method, not evidence. Mentat's PAC transfer graph follows only FEC-reported committee cash, so it cannot see the nonprofit layer this paper maps. The retired cosponsor InfluenceScore has the same shape as the paper's composite: a hand-weighted mix of centralities led by out-degree. Neither the paper nor the system checks such a composite against an outcome. The paper's AHP consistency ratio and one-weight sensitivity sweep are reusable ways to document owner-judgment weights such as the pillar blend. They do not make those weights valid. The game theory section has no counterpart in the system.

bearings.paper_claim: The dark money network is a money-flow graph among 501(c) nonprofits and SMLLCs. Ties mean funds exchanged and tie width is the dollar amount. Its defining feature is unlimited donations with no donor disclosure. The authors map it from news and IRS sources from 2010-2014, not from FEC filings. The top node, Freedom Partners Chamber of Commerce, has out-degree 90.

Opposition stays with the named target. The docstring says the result is a conditional pro-rata scenario, not traced dollars. Nothing upstream of a reporting committee enters the graph.

Industry money that passes through a non-disclosing nonprofit before reaching a super PAC appears in FEC data, at most, as one contributor row naming the nonprofit, so its sources are invisible to Mentat. The paper gives no data source or method for that hidden layer: its edges come from journalism. The network is from about 2010-2015 and is a single partisan donor network. Do not import its centrality ranking as evidence about any industry Mentat tracks. Any key-node ranking on Mentat's committee graph would be a heuristic output (D-025).

gaps_exposed: Mentat has no non-disclosing nonprofit (501(c)(4)/(c)(6), SMLLC) layer upstream of reporting committees. Industry money routed through such conduits enters the transfer graph only at the receiving committee, so attributed industry totals are a lower bound on that channel. The paper shows this layer exists and is organized as a network.

No recorded weight-sensitivity sweep exists for the four-pillar blend. A one-weight-at-a-time proportional-rescale sweep (paper Eq. 1) is a cheap answer to the open question on top-133 overlap between weight sets.

Owner-judgment tables (pillar weights, IMP weights, SGATE, PERS) have no documented elicitation or internal-consistency check. AHP's consistency ratio is one way to record that judgments are at least coherent. It would not validate them.
Neither the paper nor the system validates a weighted-centrality composite against an outcome. The retired InfluenceScore still feeds the underdog lens without such a test.
flags: D-025: the paper calls TOPSIS output a 'closeness coefficient' and frames high scorers as key or influential nodes. If any of this is ported, label it a heuristic model output: not network closeness, access, or influence probability.
The paper's weights and game payoffs are the authors' own Saaty-scale judgments with no external validation. Do not cite it as evidence that out-degree should dominate a centrality composite.
The 10-strategy nonlinear-program solution as printed is internally inconsistent: x2 = 0.92 and x4 = 0.8 sum to 1.72. Do not quote it.
The game's premise contains a partisan framing of the State player, which is the authors' assumption, not a finding. Keep it out of any Melange or Mentat surface.

This analysis is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). Neither rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization) is argued for here. Tie width = dollars is display, not normalization.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotations on this paper. The component list cites it only as 'on disk' under the PAC transfer graph, next to his note linking dark-money giving to Furnas's ideological infrastructure. The paper supports the idea that a dark-money organization network is real and can be mapped. It also shows that this network sits upstream of anything Mentat's FEC-only graph can trace, which his notes do not address. On centrality, Paul says more research on forms of centrality is needed. The paper's answer is to weight several centralities by expert judgment (AHP/TOPSIS), but it never validates the result. It therefore does not resolve his question and does not reverse the system's retirement of direction-blind centrality. His Sotoudeh highlight (eigenvector is 'not a strong indicator of bill passage') remains the more relevant evidence.

related.why: Irvin investigates how dark money operates across US nonprofit advocacy organizations. That is the population this paper samples one network from, and it can give the scope and prevalence this single-network study lacks.
Sotoudeh tests whether cosponsorship centrality predicts bill passage. That outcome validation is exactly what the AHP/TOPSIS composite here never does.
Both papers face the same choice of which centrality to use. Ardekani picks Katz on substantive grounds, while this paper weights eight centralities by expert judgment.
Gaynor builds directed money-flow networks among political organizations (leadership PACs to caucus members), the same kind of financial-tie object this paper analyzes for nonprofits.
Ringe et al. treat network centrality as a measure of political influence. Their work is a contrast case for whether a centrality ranking stands for real power, which this paper simply assumes.
